train.c1: Persuasive writing in grant writing (US focus)
train.c1.desc: A highly interactive, workshop-style course on NIH grant applications, aimed at US-based researchers. It is organised in six modules and can be delivered flexibly, either as a three-day intensive or spread over several weeks. Exercises take place in small breakout groups, so participants have more time to discuss their work and get to know colleagues from other parts of the institution. The facilitators then lead a plenary discussion with the whole group. A 30-minute one-to-one session with personalised feedback on the participant's own abstract can be arranged on request.
train.c2: Persuasive writing in grant writing (EU focus)
train.c2.desc: A highly interactive, workshop-style course on grant applications for researchers based in the UK and Europe. The examples and exercises draw on ERC, Horizon Europe (including MSCA fellowships), UKRI, Wellcome and NIHR applications. The course is organised in six modules and can be delivered flexibly, either as a three-day intensive or spread over several weeks. Exercises take place in small breakout groups, so participants have more time to discuss their work and get to know colleagues from other parts of the institution. The facilitators then lead a plenary discussion with the whole group. A 30-minute one-to-one session with personalised feedback on the participant's own abstract can be arranged on request.

j.title: Journal Launch & Growth
j.lead: We help research institutions turn scientific strength into internationally competitive journals.
j.why: Many institutional journals start with excellent science and then stall: too few strong submissions, an unclear scope, a board that exists on paper, policies that indexers will not accept.
j.cred: We have built a journal from the first issue. Simona Fiorani was launching Editor in Chief of iScience. She was also a team leader at Nature Communications and a senior editor at Nature Cell Biology.
jp1.q: Should this journal exist, and who will read, cite and submit to it?
jp1.1: Map of competing journals: scope, model and indexation status
jp1.2: Evidence of author demand from your own and peer institutions
jp1.3: A go / no-go report with the costs of running the journal
jp2.q: Where can your institution’s strength own a gap in the field?
jp2.1: Aims and scope, article types and audience
jp2.3: Business model options: diamond open access or APC-funded
jp3.q: Who gives the journal international credibility from day one?
jp3.1: Board structure, roles and terms of reference
jp3.2: Candidates balanced by region, career stage and gender
jp3.3: Invitation materials and onboarding for new editors
jp4.q: How do you build the content, reach and record that indexers look for?
jp4.1: COPE-aligned editorial and ethics policies, peer-review workflow
jp4.2: Content plan: commissioned reviews, special issues, launch papers
jp4.3: Outreach to authors, reviewers and readers
jp4.4: A milestone map to each index, then the application dossier
ja.p: A fixed-scope review of an existing journal: submissions and turnaround, board activity, policies, website and metadata, measured against indexation criteria. You get a ranked action plan, whether the journal is new or was turned down by an index.
ji.who: Inclusion is always the indexer’s decision
ji.p: We make the journal ready and build a record that stands up to review. We never sell guaranteed indexation.
j.cta: Each phase can be bought on its own. Start with feasibility and decide after the report.
